---
title: Correcting a price
description: The only route from a vendor to a published price — how a proposal is reviewed, how it is labelled once live, and why it can never be overwritten by automation.
---

You are the authority on what you charge. You are also an interested party in how it is
displayed beside your competitors. The price proposal is how both of those stay true at
once.

**Owners never write a price directly.** There is no field, no API and no admin route that
takes a vendor's number straight to a published page. A proposal is the only path, and it
passes a person.

## Proposing

From [your listings](/my-listings), on a tool you have
[claimed](/docs/vendors/claiming-a-listing), propose the corrected figure: the amount, its
currency, the unit it is charged in, the billing period, and whether it is an overage rate.

Give the **source** — your own published pricing page, ideally. A proposal that points at a
public page is quick to approve. One that does not needs a human to establish the fact some
other way, which is slower but not refused.

You can withdraw a proposal while it is pending.

## What review does

An editor checks the figure against whatever public evidence exists and publishes it, or
comes back to you. What lands on the page then carries two permanent properties:

**It is labelled 🏷 Supplied by the vendor, not independently verified.** That wording is
fixed. It is not a comment on your honesty — it is an accurate statement about what we did
and did not check, and it is the disclosure that makes accepting vendor input safe at all.

**It is pinned.** Our automated price reader can never silently overwrite it. A figure a
person decided on stays decided until another person changes it.

## What a proposal closes

A published proposal closes the matching slot only — the same **currency, billing period
and overage flag**. A metered plan with a $15 monthly fee and a $0.05 per-page overage rate
holds two current prices, and correcting the monthly fee leaves the overage rate exactly
where it was. If both are wrong, propose both.

## What we will not publish

- A trial presented as a free tier.
- An annual-prepay rate described as a monthly one.
- A per-seat price described as a flat one.
- A cap you have not published, whether generous or restrictive.

These are not judgements about your pricing. They are the four ways a comparison table
most often misleads, and they are refused regardless of who supplies the number, us
included. The full statement is in [the methodology](/docs/methodology#what-we-will-not-do).
